Gravity

0000: Gravity

Throughout your life, you will find yourself pulled by many things. Gravity is always drawing you somewhere. If you don't pay attention, you will end up in a place you never decided to go. Sometimes that's a good place. You can drift for years and settle into an orbit around something warm. But sometimes it is a dark place. Where you are most likely to end up depends on your environment. And for many of the people reading this, the environment is changing. Darkness has always pulled at people. But more mass and energy is accumulating around things designed to seduce. More and more, drifting ends in the same place. I am at a point in my life where I realize I have been captured. There wasn't one dramatic moment when it happened. But when I look out at the world, everything is moving faster than it should. Time is moving right past me. And when I look ahead I can see the abyss, and the point past which there is no return. It feels natural to ask myself what decisions led me here. I can name some, but that alone does not get me out. You cannot fight gravity. The one decision you can start with is what to orient yourself towards, and let that pull you. So that is my vow. I will not drift. I will turn towards light and beauty. I am writing this to make that vow public and expensive. And not to stop here, but to build something that is made to last. Something that can be a light for others to turn towards.

0001: Form & Time

The foundation of this project is a small text file that declares what kinds of things exist.

In software, a file like this is called a schema. A schema defines the shape things are allowed to take and what a valid instance of each kind must have. Everything downstream is built against those definitions instead of fuzzy, unspoken ones.

I don't think of this file as just a technical artifact. It is more like a grammar. Before a community can create things together, it needs a shared understanding of what exists. It is an agreement that sits underneath every other agreement. Usually that agreement stays implicit, and implicit agreements drift. Writing this grammar down as a canonical, enforceable text is what turns the agreement into real infrastructure. Something that can be referenced, built on, and argued against.

Concretely, the file currently defines two types: Weeks and Cycles. Before naming any of the things that will be created, the grammar names the time they will be made in. Traditionally, communities are constituted by shared time before shared things.

A Week is the grid: uniform, repeating, the same size every time. That sameness is the point. A Week exists to carry rhythm like rituals, check-ins, and habits that only work because the interval never changes. You feel a sense of belonging because your time has the same shape as everyone else's.

A Cycle is the arc: time defined by its purpose. A Cycle exists to produce one primary creative output.

0002: The Lifecycle of Software Objects

Every Sunday, this project will publish a record of everything that changed in the week behind it.

0000 was a vow. 0001 was the grammar. But a vow you cannot check is only a feeling, and drift never announces itself. That Sunday record is the machinery: it turns orientation into something you can verify instead of something you assume. A few new kinds of things have to exist before it can be written.

Three new types will be introduced:

  1. Post
  2. Change
  3. Release

A Post is a published piece of writing. It exists to state intent. Before the project changes in a way that matters, the reasoning has to be written down and made public, where it can be read and argued against. Going with the flow is another name for gravity. A Post is the act of deciding instead of being pulled.

A Change is a single alteration to the project. Every Change has a magnitude: major, minor, or patch. This is borrowed from general software versioning. Patches fix, minors add, and majors alter what the thing is. Naming the magnitude is a small act of judgment, made in the open, every time. The point is not precision. The point is a shared language for how the thing moves. Every Change carries its own record, so nothing lands unexplained; the Post is reserved for the ones that change what this is.

A Release is an end of week ritual. Weeks run Monday to Sunday, so a Release lands on the day off: a weekly act of record gathering every Change that landed that week. It is the point where the week stops being private effort and becomes something witnessed. A week with nothing in it still gets a Release. An empty Release is drift, dated and visible.

Major Changes only ship after a Post about it has been published. The Post states the intent and the rationale for the Change. This makes majors expensive on purpose. They should be rare, and they should cost something to make.

This post is a major Change. Three new types alter what this is. So it ships the only way a major can, written down first.
